en: [Siddham] Homage to Vāgīśvara.
[Success! With all three bodies, I bow to that which is equal to space, the supreme primordial one, for the sake of its meaning.
I am composing a commentary on this tantra,
which is equal to space, that is itself equal to space.
In this context, the Blessed One Vajradhara is the enlightenment (bodhi) of all Buddhas, and that [enlightenment] is characterized by the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti).
The basis is the body, and it is threefold for them.

In that regard, as long as there is a basis characterized by the mental continuum—which serves as the substratum for the seeds of defiled phenomena and their latencies known as *dauṣṭhulya*—it is called the *ālayavijñāna*. Subsequently, through the Noble Path, which is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) and has been cultivated for a long time, those [seeds] are completely exhausted. Consequently, for that which is no longer called the *ālaya*, there occurs the cessation of those representations (*vijñapti*) appearing as the physical world, the body, and objects of enjoyment, as well as the absolute cessation of other arisen defiled phenomena and the non-arising of those not yet arisen.

Because of its non-arising, there is a rule of cessation with respect to that nature. However, because it is like the pure sky—non-conceptual, luminous by nature, and infinite—there is a rule of activity. This is the revolution (parāvṛtti). That is the revolution of the basis of the depravities (dauṣṭhulya) for the Buddhas; it alone is called their untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu), because it is the locus of the seeds of the untainted Buddha-qualities. It is also the path that serves as their basis. Its revolution is the absolute cessation of the worldling’s form.

And there is an ultimate engagement by means of the supramundane. The suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena is also their basis. Its revolution (*parāvṛtti*) is the ultimate purification of all adventitious obscurations. This very revolution of the Buddhas—the basis of depravity, the basis of the path, and the basis of suchness—is their enlightenment (*bodhi*), and that itself is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Because it is the body and the support of the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*), it is called the "essential body" (*svābhāvikakāya*). This is because it abides eternally in the very nature of suchness (*tathatā*) and luminosity (*prakāśa*). Thus, this Blessed One Vajradhara, characterized by the awakening of a Buddha, is by nature equal to space. His nature is his essential body; therefore, he is indeed equal to space, for he has suchness as his intrinsic nature, consisting of infinite, perfectly pure luminosities that are free from all appearances.

Although the Enjoyment Body (*sāṃbhogika-kāya*) is not literally equal to space due to its manifold forms, it is nevertheless equal to space according to its appearance. For the Dharma Body experiences phenomena as unobstructed through its reality that is equal to space; the Enjoyment Body likewise discerns them, because it is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of that experience. And how does it discern them in such a way? By discerning them through the non-existence of the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and their appearances.

For example, the determination of fools regarding the experience of a jar or similar objects occurs through its existence (*sattā*). Just as the vivid experience of the form of a jar by fools determines it as existing—even without verbal expression—it does so by means of existence alone, due to the force of the latencies (*vāsanā*) from the repeated practice of prior determinations. In the same way, the non-conceptual *saṃbhogakāya* of the Buddhas determines its own form precisely through non-existence (*asattā*). This very determination is what is intended here by the term "appearance" (*pratibhāsa*).
For manifestation is of two kinds: direct experience and secondary indication. Therefore, even the Saṃbhogakāya of the Buddhas is, according to its manifestation, equal to space.

The emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), however, is even more like space; for even by illusionists, a person or the like created by themselves is perceived precisely through its non-existence. And that Vajradhara is the progenitor of all Buddhas, while they too are like space because they are his outflow—this is the established tenet.

1.1 An objection to this established doctrine: Vajradhara is not at all the progenitor of the Buddhas; rather, he is a son of the Buddhas because of his crown of five Buddhas. Since he is the union of body, speech, and mind with that wheel of goddesses, he is merely a conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and one who sets in motion the method of proliferation. He is neither equal to space nor a proponent of the method of equality with space. To refute this objection, he says: "The five Buddhas," and so forth.
On this point there are two verses:
"In this [system], the *gaṇa* consists of two, three, four, five, or six *mātrās*, and is thus fivefold;
generally, a *dvipadī* metre has a quarter-verse (*pāda*) consisting of three or four *gaṇas*."
In this context, Apabhraṃśa is a dialect that is a modification of Sanskrit;
its completion is achieved through short and long vowels, the bindu, and rapid or slow tempos.

*Short*, *long*, *bindu*, *dvipadī*, *khaṇḍa*, and *vastuka* are synonyms. Among these, in the first type, *dvipadī*, there are three *gaṇas* per foot. In the odd feet (*ayukpāda*), the first *gaṇa* consists of six *mātrās*; the second consists of two *mātrās*; and the remaining [two] consist of four *mātrās* each. The word *ca* (and) has its *ca*-sound elided and is displaced in the sequence. There are two instances of the word *ho*. One is a substitute for *usa* (i.e., *ṅgasa*). The second is an indeclinable used in the sense of the word *khalu* or for the purpose of address. The shortening of the vowel *o* in the two instances of the word *ho* is for the sake of metrical completion.

For instance, in Apabhraṃśa, there is shortening of *e* and *o* when followed by a consonant, as well as the elision of the consonant itself according to observation—as in examples such as *jaï kĕvi*, *jaï kŏvi*, and *jaï piu*.
[Note: The commentary suggests that the consonant is elided, yet the *c* is not; thus he read *ca* instead of *a*.]

Regarding *saṃyukta* [consonant clusters]: there is shortening of *e* and *o* in the locative case when they undergo elision (*lopa*) at the end of the first member of a compound; likewise, there is shortening of consonant clusters (such as *tta*, etc., which do not cause *gaṇa*-position). This is in accordance with our empirical observation.

Perhaps it refers to a well-known verse: "In that very place, the connection is thus: he whose crown is the support of the five Buddhas and who is the essence of the three worlds—or rather, the essence of the world of women—and who has brought about the state of the Ādibuddha, his movement is indeed equal to space."
"Equal to space" refers to the movement [of the winds].

"Residing in the crown" means situated in the crown of the head. "Of whom" refers to Vajrasattva. The three secrets of body, speech, and mind, which are subsumed within the mandalas of the yogins, constitute the three worlds (*tribhuvana*). Alternatively, "woman" (*strī*) refers to the yoginīs; their world is the mandala, which is the "world of women" (*strībhuvana*), and that is whose essence and manifestation it is, because of the nature of the Vajra Way (*vajranaya*). As it is said in the *Guhyasamāja*: [The verse from the *Guhyasamāja* follows here.]
Delight in the vajra is always established within delusion, hatred, and passion;
it is known as the Vajrayāna, the skillful means of all the Buddhas.

Because he is the first of the six universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), Vajrasattva is the *Ādibuddha*. Precisely because he is a universal monarch, he possesses an even crown (*samakuṭa*) and an even maṇḍala. He is so called because he possesses a nature that is "made" (*kṛta*), "fabricated" (*kṛtaka*), and "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*). For one who exists in such a state, this activity (*pracāra*) or conventional usage (*vyavahāra*)—the conventionality consisting of his own body, speech, mind, crown, Buddhas, and so forth—is entirely equal to space (*khasama*), because it appears through its equality with space. How so? Because it is delimited by the non-existence of [inherent] forms (*ākāra*).

Therefore, this Blessed One is himself equal to space and is the promulgator of the Vajra Way, which is equal to space. Even his own crown-deity Buddha was created by him alone; how much more so the emanated Buddhas? Thus, he is indeed the progenitor of the Buddhas.
But is he not also called a "son of the Buddha"? How is that? Sometimes, because he has the form of a Bodhisattva; for Bodhisattvas are the sons of the Buddhas. (1.2)

[Objection: "In the Mantra system (*mantranīti*), the body, speech, and mind of the Blessed One, as well as the maṇḍala, are meditated upon. Therefore, there can be no attainment of the *dharmakāya*, which is devoid of appearances (*nirābhāsa*). If that is not attained, then the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, which depend upon it, will certainly not be attained either. If, on the other hand, its meditation is of a different nature, then let that be explained. To this he says: *jaï* and so forth. Regarding the [metrical] feet (*kāya*) here, the *gaṇas* consist of exactly four morae (*mātrā*). In the odd feet (*ayukpāda*), there are four; in the even feet (*yukpāda*), there are three. Both *e* and *eṃ* are short *e*-vowels (*ekāra*). The *bindu* is very small.

The mind is examined by means of the first state; this is the state of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Indeed, the nature of a Buddha is not seen, nor is it the nature of consciousness. By "by this"—meaning by what is to be stated in the second half [of the verse]—"by means of the state" (*bhāvena*) means by way of a mode; thus the mind of the yogin is ceased and concentrated. This is the meditation on Vajrasattva as ultimate reality; there is no other.

To the question "By what kind of cultivation? he says "Buddha," and so forth. That which is external to the mind and graspable by the mind is its intrinsic nature; thus, it is indeed of the nature of a Buddha (*buddhasvabhāva*). However, that is neither seen, nor apprehended, nor conceptualized, nor is it the real form (*ākāra*) of the intrinsic nature of consciousness, because it cannot withstand analysis as being either one or many. For in this way, the non-apprehension of the grasped and the grasper is the cause for attaining the *dharmakāya*, whose nature is the non-apprehension of duality. The cultivation of body, speech, and mind, however, pertains to the *saṃbhogakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Therefore, this alone is its cultivation, because it brings about the three bodies more swiftly.
1.3 Let it be that such is the visualization for Vajradhara; but how is the visualization for the Buddhas and others? To this he says: "buddhassa," and so forth.

Here, there are four *gaṇas* in each quarter-verse (*pāda*). In the first quarter, the first two [syllables] have two and three morae (*mātrās*) respectively. In the even quarters, the first has six morae, the second has two morae, and the remaining [syllables] have four morae each.

Of the Buddha, the Vajra-holder, the Jewel-bannered one, who is accompanied by Padmā and surrounded [by deities]—of these gods there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The Primordial Buddha (*Ādibuddha*) is space; that is the intrinsic nature.

"Of the Buddhas" refers to Vairocana; "of the Vajra-holder" refers to Akṣobhya; "of Ratnaketu" refers to Ratnasambhava; "by Padma" refers to Amitābha; and "of the Circular One" means of Amoghasiddhi. "Of these" refers to the five Tathāgatas. "Of the gods" refers to the goddesses and their families. "There is no intrinsic nature" because the duality of the appearance of the grasped and the grasper is unreal.

If the duality is false, what then is their own nature? "Ādibuddha" refers to Vajradhara; "ākāśa" refers to that which is equal to space (*khasama*), because it has the characteristic of the *dharmakāya* and because it shines forth through its equality with space. This is their own being; it is their own nature, because they are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of that [nature]. To summarize this, he says: "Āi," and so forth.

Here too, there are four *gaṇas* per quarter. In the first quarter, the first two are six-mora (*ṣaṭmātra*) and two-mora (*dvimātra*) respectively; likewise in the fourth. In the third, the first is two-mora, and the remaining [three] are four-mora each.
Regarding "this" (*eṣa*), it means "this one" (*eṣā*).
Regarding "upajja," the doubling of the letter *p* is not desired.

*Upajjaï?* [is it so? The word *khaïm* is protracted, consisting of three morae (*trimātra*). From the word *kha*, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), resulting in *khaka*. There remains only the vowel. The singular instrumental ending *-in* becomes *-i*, and the vowel *a* is elided. This is the origin of the primary dharma (*ādidharma*). Sentient beings (*sattvāḥ*) arise as equal to the void (*khena*). Although there is plurality, the singular number is employed; in this system, the treatise (*śāstra*) is the authority (*pramāṇa*).

The primordial pure state is that of those who are equal to space. The primordial dharma is Vajrasattva, because his nature is the Dharmakāya. This is his arising through body, speech, and mind, which are equal to space.
[What is meant by "equal" (samāna)?]

Its arising is indeed its manifestation through the destruction of all obscurations without exception, like the arising of space from the demolition of a palace. Space is the sign and the illustrative example for its arising. Thus it is said in the *Śrīparamādya*:
"Because he is the sign of the arising of space, the Supreme is without beginning or end;
the Being consisting of all vajras, Vajrasattva, is supreme bliss."

Thus [it is said]. For this very reason, beings such as Buddhas arise, because they are delimited by the non-existence of formal characteristics (*ākāra*); they are equal to space (*kha*). If it is objected: "In the Yoga Tantras, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā alone is enlightenment (*bodhi*). Knowledge equal to space is merely its cause, not its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, there is a contradiction between the *Khasamata-tantra* and all the Yoga Tantras," he replies with the words beginning with "the method" (*naya*). A "method" (*naya*) is that by which something is led or explained. That Blessed One by whom the sūtras of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) are explained is the "method."

Even though that reality is not established through letters, the scripture—the Blessed One’s teaching—is accepted as the authority, and not its opposite. Now, regarding the method (*naya*) concerning mantra, mudrā, and so forth, which possess form within cognition, he says: "Primordial," and so on. "Primordial purity" (*ādiśuddhi*) is the *dharmakāya*. That itself is the state (*pada*), the objective support (*ālambana*). Because mantras, mudrās, and so forth—which are equal to space and have space as their natural outflow (*niṣyanda*)—appear as being equal to space, they are like space. For this very reason, this is the *uttaratantra* among all tantras. It is also stated in the *Śrīsarvarahasyatantra*:
There is indeed no reality of cause, nor likewise any reality of fruit;
that reality is the knowledge of suchness, wherein the yogi should practice.

Thus: the reality of the cause consists of four aspects, beginning with the penetration of the mind; the reality of the fruit is the fifth aspect. Both of these are non-existent according to their own forms. The reality of those two is precisely the knowledge of suchness (*tathatājñāna*), because it delimits them through the non-existence of their own forms. The meaning is that the yogi should practice within that delimitation. It is also stated in the *Śrīsamāja*: "The body is the unarisen syllable; speech and mind are without characteristics."
It is a false collection, consisting of the conceptualization of space as vajra.

Thus: it is called the "imperishable" (*akṣara*) because it does not decay; it is the secret—the secret of body, the secret of speech, and the secret of mind. All that appears as unarisen and without intrinsic nature, because it is delimited by its non-existence according to its form. Within the space-vajra, the *dharmakāya*, which is experienced as the fluidity of phenomena (*dharmadrava*), that which consists of conceptual construction and has the nature of delimitation is delimited by reality as being equal to space, both through its existence and through its non-existence according to its form. And that is false because it possesses form; yet it is also a synthesis.

Because it is correctly discerned, it is so described as being "comprised by that. The meaning is that it is comprised by pure mundane knowledge (*śuddhalaukikajñāna*). Thus far, the meditation on the equality of space (*khasamārthabhāvanā*), which is common to all Yoga Tantras, has been explained.
Now, in order to introduce the meditation on the equality of space that is common specifically to the *Śrīsamāja* and other tantras, he says "five," and so forth; this consists of two couplets.
By the first [word], it is equal in number.
The first word *ca* has the sense of "also" (*api*). The second is for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and its position is displaced.
He whose very nature (*svabhāva*) is the Dharma, even though he possesses the crown of the five Buddhas.

Vajrasattva, whose power is the Dharma of the three worlds, should be saluted. Vajrasattva should be saluted. Of what nature is he? He is one for whom, even while possessing a body, the *dharmakāya* alone is the essential nature (*svabhāva*). This is because he reveals himself through that very form—the *dharmakāya*, which is like space and consists of all the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*) having attained a state of equal flavor (*samarasībhūta*). Furthermore, of what nature is he? The "three worlds" (*tribhuvana*) refers to the circle of yoginīs (*yoginīcakra*). He is so described because his power of Dharma (*dharmaprabhāva*)—characterized by the teaching of the Dharma and the enjoyment of the Dharma—belongs to him. And it is said in the *Śrīvajraśikhara*:
Then, having again emanated the natural bodies through the enjoyment [bodies], [he remains]. Thus.

In this context, meditative cultivation alone is intended as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Prostration consists of the entry of one’s own body, speech, and mind into the body, speech, and mind of that [deity].
[3r] "One's own body" is what is intended.
He speaks of the benefit of prostration with the words beginning with "vajra": when Vajrasattva is prostrated to, merit also becomes infinite;
by prostrating to Vajrasattva, the greatness of the Dharma is attained.

"Merit also"—by the word "also," knowledge as well [is included]. "Infinite" means as much as would constitute the complete accumulation of the provisions (*saṃbhāra*). Furthermore, one should prostrate again, because from prostration one obtains the greatness of the Dharma and the majesty of Vajradhara. In some manuscripts, the word *svabhāva* (nature) is read in place of *mahattva* (greatness); in that case, there is no occurrence of the poetic figure *yamaka* (rhyme/parallelism). That too is not a fault, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). [Is it] because of the possibility of deviation?

1.7 It has been stated that the *dharmakāya* itself attains the state of being the body of Vajrasattva. In that regard, the *dharmakāya*, though not directly perceived, is to be meditated upon by means of a symbolic convention (*saṃketa*). He explains this with the words beginning with "all" (*sarva*), etc.
[Is it "savva," etc.?]
This too is that same *dvipadī* (two-footed verse); however, it is performed with two feet.
Having cultivated all sentient beings, the nature of liberation is produced.

Having summoned all the perfectly awakened ones (*saṃbuddha*) by means of the sounds of illusory passion (*māyāsurata*), and having caused them to enter and dissolve into the heart, one visualizes them as situated within the interior of the lotus; thus the nature of liberation is produced—white like the melting autumn moon, the *dharmakāya*, which is the state of equal flavor (*samarasībhāva*) of all the qualities of a Buddha.
1.8 Then, he asks what is to be done next and says "vajra," etc.
Here, there are four quarters consisting of four gaṇas each.
A note on the "6 + 2" regarding the first "4 + 4":
Liberation is made by Vajrasattva through the nature of all things; it is the nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*).
And this phenomenon is of an indestructible nature.

How, then, is he made into an embodied being? To this he says: "By the world," and so forth. "By the world" means by way of a cause for the sake of the world; that is, he is made—that is, manifested—in another nature, in the form of Vajrasattva. This is because [the form] is perceived by those to be trained (*vineya*) through transformation according to convention. However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), it is simply another cognition, which is an outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the Dharma-body, that arises in that form; and it appears to the Blessed One as having no existence in accordance with that form.
1.9 From here onwards, that same *dvipadī* consists of three *gaṇas* per foot, until before the verse beginning with "e caü devī."
"Kāya," and so forth. Here, the shortening of the vowels in the words *uppatti* and *pakārāṇāṃ* is for the sake of metrical completion.
"Body, speech, and therein mind—O, the first arising of the Dharma.
The Yoga-pīṭha; therein the goddess Cundā is the arising of the Dharma.

If it is asked, "In that generation of Vajrasattva, what is his origin and what is the place of his generation? he says: This triad of body, speech, and mind is the primordial generation of the Dharma-Vajrasattva.
Cundā Bhagavatī, the Great Body, is the seat and the foundation of yoga; therein occurs the generation of Vajrasattva.
He asks: who are his mother and father, and how is his birth? He says: "Vajra-ho," and so forth.
"Vajra-ho" is a six-mora (*ṣaṭmātra*) metrical unit drawn out with a slow tempo.
Therein, the mantra-practitioner meditates upon [the deity] as having a single nature with the Vajra.
One takes as an object and contemplates the form of the Dharma, which has the nature of a vajra.

"Of the vajra" means of Akṣobhya. "On that yoga-seat" [refers to that place]. "Of one nature" means that because it is conjoined with the *svābhāvikī* (innate) wisdom, it is both "one" (*ekā*) and "of its own nature" (*svabhāvā*); thus, it is "that which is one and of its own nature. "The form of the Dharma" refers to liberation, as before. "The nature of a vajra" refers to the arising of the body of Vajrasattva.
He describes that very [deity] with the words beginning with "jaṭā":
adorned with a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭa*), and having a complexion whose nature is blue.
This practitioner meditates upon the perfect samādhi of Vajrasattva with devotion;

he beholds the Blessed One adorned with a crown of matted hair resplendent with the five Buddhas. His color is blue. In this manner, one should correctly meditate upon the samādhi of Vajrasattva. "This" refers to the yogin. "With devotion" (sabhāvaḥ) means together with devotion—that is, with reverence. However, the crown of matted hair of Akṣobhya has the single jewel symbol on the outside, not the Buddha symbols.
Now, does Akṣobhya also arise from the melting of the moon? No, he says: "Akka," and so forth.
"Akka" is a group of three morae; "majjhaṭṭhiu" consists of five morae.
One contemplates the arising of the syllables situated within the orb of the sun.
Having brought forth the form of the syllable, one contemplates it as having the nature of a vajra.
"Arka" means the sun. The syllable is the blue *hūṃ*. The seed-syllable of Vajrasattva, however, is the white *hūṃ*. "The nature of a vajra" refers to the form of Akṣobhya.
1.13 It is said that the arising of Vajrasattva also occurs from mantra alone, beginning with *jalataum* and so forth.
Here, the first group [of syllables] should be made four mātras in length by means of rapid pronunciation.
The mantra-practitioner meditates on that which arises within the water as the essential nature of his own form. Does he meditate on form as the essential nature?

One takes as one’s object Vajrasattva, whose intrinsic nature is non-dual form. That very [nature] is like water or the flow of a moon; it exists within sentient beings and within their parents, and from that it is born. This means that it is the form of the self, its own intrinsic nature, the seed-syllable of one’s own deity. The practitioner visualizes that [seed-syllable] situated in the center of the moon-maṇḍala; by means of that seed-syllable, he visualizes Vajrasattva, whose intrinsic nature is the non-dual body. How is the body non-dual? Because there is no appearance of "object" nor "cognition," or because of union with one's own consort (*svavidyā*). (1.14)
Concluding the yoga, he states its fruit, beginning with "This," and so forth:
"This accomplishment of the mind has been taught by Vajradhara.
He who meditates with this state of being succeeds as the very nature of the mind."

The perfection of the mind is the yoga of the mind of Vajradhara. By means of "cultivation" (bhāvena)—that is, by way of this method—one meditates upon Vajrasattva; he becomes perfected as the very nature of the mind of Vajradhara.

1.15 If [it is argued that] even for Vajradhara there is no arising from mantra because it is impossible for one established in the non-conceptual (*aprapañca*) samādhi to produce a body, then his emergence from that samādhi—being unimpelled—would necessarily be a distraction (*vikṣepa*) or a state lacking a leader (*anāyakadharma*). To this, he says: "e" and so forth.
Here, in each quarter-verse (*pāda*), there are four groups (*gaṇa*) of four morae (*mātrā*).
Again, something is missing; the third *pāda* consists of six and two syllables, while the fourth consists of four and four.
This single-natured goddess of the four deities manifests her own nature through song.
Thus, she manifests the Dharma, whose nature is the cultivated mind, as the goddess whose nature is liberation.

"Fourfold goddess" means the group of four goddesses. "Of a single nature" means having the form of liberation (*mokṣa*). "By song" refers to the four songs that will be explained below. "Bhāva" means intention; "he brings that about" (*bhāvayati*) means he causes it to arise by generating the intention of the mantra-form, which is to say, he awakens it. Which one does he awaken? "By *kha*," meaning its own nature, its common nature, or that which is equal to space—namely, the fluid of phenomena (*dharmadrava*).

The word *eva* has this meaning and must be brought from the Prakrit; for even Prakrit enters into Apabhraṃśa, as in examples such as *janto ccia* and *tanto ccia*. This being so, the yogin meditates upon the flow of dharma as having the nature of the composed mind, having the form of Vajradhara, and likewise the form of the Goddess, whose nature is liberation. The intention is that the perfectly pure mind is Vajrasattva, and perfectly pure suchness is the Goddess.

In order to provide himself as an example for the point that Buddhahood is attained through this meditation, a certain Buddha, having assembled his retinue, spoke even though the meaning had not been explicitly stated: "Vajrasattva," and so forth. In these two lines, there are three *gaṇas* in each foot. There is a doubling of the syllable *pī* in the word *pīṭha*, while there is no doubling of the syllable *pa* in the word *utpatti*. Regarding *upattiho*: a four-moraic unit is formed by a short vowel followed by a *druta* (quick) consonant. "I have seen Vajrasattva rejoicing in the *yogapīṭha*."
Having taken a wife who is entirely equal to himself, he remains wearing her attire. Indeed, from his own nature, there is an arising of existence;
therein, Vajrasattva—who has been perceived—enters and, being seated, emanates the Buddhas.

"Dārām" means the wife. "Sakalasamām" means she is identical in all respects to the Blessed One. For just as the Blessed One is blue, with a crown of matted hair adorned by the five Buddhas, holding a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) in his right hand and a bell marked with a crossed-vajra in his left, so too does this Blessed Lady stand. "Yaḥ" (who) is the understood subject. "Veṣaḥ" refers to her attire or adornment.

"From its own nature" (*sabhāvāt*) means from its common nature (*samānabhāvāt*). "From existence" (*bhāvāt*) means from the reality (*tattva*) of all sentient beings; the meaning is "from the essence of phenomena" (*dharmadrava*). "He plunges into" (*avagāhate*) means he discerns (*paricchinatti*); the word "that" (*tām*) is to be supplied as the object. To the question "How? he says: "He expands," and so forth. "Established with the mind" (*niviṣṭo manasā*) means concentrated (*samāhita*). "Caü," and so forth.
Here, the odd quarters consist of three *gaṇas*, while the even quarters consist of two *gaṇas*. The word *jja* has the meaning of the word *khalu*.
He is situated in the midst of the four goddesses who possess the nature of the four [elements].
He has entered the three worlds through the nature of *māyā*.

The infinite distinctions of body, speech, mind, and their respective activities for each of all the Buddhas are condensed into four secrets: the secret of body, the secret of mind, the secret of speech, and the secret of activity. Their suchness (*tathatā*) is, respectively, the four goddesses; therefore, they possess the four natures. For this very reason, they are white, blue, red, and green. With their right hands, they hold vajras of their own corresponding color; with their left hands, they hold a wheel, a red utpala, a lotus, and a blue utpala. They wear jeweled crowns adorned by the Tathāgata of their own family.

Seated upon a vajra-paryaṅka in their midst, because they appear as being like an illusion; by them the three worlds are encompassed; having entered and plunged into the three secrets of the Tathāgata as being like an illusion, he discerns them.
1.19 From here onwards, there are three *dvipadikās*. Each quarter-verse (*pāda*) consists of four *gaṇas*, but the third [quarter] consists of two *pādas*.
[The rule begins with] "excluding *vissa*," and so forth.

There, upon that [moon], is the universal vajra with four faces belonging to the deity Vajradhara. “There” means on the moon at the heart. Even all the Buddhas perform this miraculous transformation (*vikurvaṇa*) for him; for this very reason, there is an emanation (*spharaṇa*) from them.

He states the utility of the emanating Buddhas: “In whatever way they arise. “Deity” (*deva*) means having become a god. “Ho” is used as a vocative. Indeed, the Buddhas possess every kind of miraculous power (*vikurvaṇa*). “He” is the understood subject.

% Devas? 1.20. Let there be the miraculous manifestation (*vikurvitam*) of Viśvavajra and of the Buddhas; but what [is the power] of Vajrasattva? To this he says: *savvaü*, etc. "Of all the gods" means of the Buddhas and so forth. *Āma* is the state of being (*umbhāvaḥ*). *Jupattī* is that which is the arising (*utpattiḥ*).
*jupattī* is an emendation; the manuscript reads *jupantī*.
Regarding *vajjasattaho*, this is the substitution (*ho-bhāva*) for the word *iti*. Regarding *tettī*, the meaning is "all that" (*tat sarvam*).
[Is it perhaps *ṅso*?]
All that is, in short, the very miraculous manifestation (*vikurvaṇa*) of Vajrasattva; the meaning is that it arises from Vajrasattva himself in those various forms.
And therefore:
"The nature of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva*) is seen everywhere."
The entire three worlds are of this very nature.

Everything that appears, such as the universal vajra and so forth, is seen as nothing but phenomena; its very nature is non-dual gnosis alone, because of the discernment that there is neither an object nor a [subjective] cognition. For this very reason, the three worlds are the circle of yoginīs. Or rather, the entire universe in its totality is seen as having but a single nature.
Regarding the verse beginning with *krīḍā*: "While playing, I saw the Buddha and all those who are masters of yoga."
"Deva," and so forth. "Deva" refers to Vajrasattva and the others; their *samaya* is their reality (*tattva*), and the chapter that illuminates it is [called] *paṭala*.

Regarding "ādimaüṃ": *ādimaḥ* means first; the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*), and there is an optional substitution of *u* for *ma*. Thus: *āimaüṃ*. Likewise: *vidijjauṃ*, *taïjjaüṃ*, *catutthaüṃ*, *pañcamaüṃ*.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Khasamā*, the commentary on the *Khasamatantra*. || 0 ||

2.1 In some places the Goddess is recited, while in others there are four goddesses. Therefore, in order to eliminate doubt regarding the number of goddesses, they ask about the number of goddesses with the words beginning "āikkha" (tell us).
Here, the odd [pādas] consist of two syllables each of six mātrās, and the even [pādas] consist of two syllables each of ten mātrās.

The connection is: "Tell [me] of the goddesses of the *samaya*-maṇḍala. "In your supreme *samaya*, how many goddesses are there? "O *sadottama*. O *sadottama*: the supreme (*uttamā*) is the principal goddess; because she is always (*sadā*) joined with the supreme within this, he is called *sadottama*. The compiler of the collection says: "There," and so forth.
This [verse] consists of three groups [of four syllables] in one quarter.

Regarding this question, the Blessed One speaks in four *gītikās*. Why? Because their names are specified right here; and because in the world it is well known that when many things are mentioned, they are presented in a sequence beginning with the principal one. This is so that the preeminence of Bhādevī and the sequential placement of the goddesses of Peace (*Śānti*) and the others in the petals of the directions starting from the East may be understood, rather than merely their number.

2.3 *suṇṇāiea* and so forth. These four songs (*gītaka*) sequentially illustrate the illusory nature (*māyopamatva*) of the secrets of mind, speech, and body. They serve to encourage the flow of the Dharma-fluid for the sake of embracing those very [secrets].

The meter here is *pramitākṣarā*. In each quarter-verse of this meter, there are four groups (*gaṇa*) of four morae (*mātrā*). The first and third groups end with a long syllable, while in the second, the long syllable occurs in the middle.
The dharmas produced by the non-discrimination of emptiness are equal to peace, liberation, and the golden age;
but in their activity, they are like illusions and equal to the Buddhas.
They sport, equal to all space and yet unquiescent—[unquiescent, as per the emendation;

*asamāḥ* in the manuscript]. Because the [gross] forms have ceased, it is "empty" (*śūnya*); and because no differentiation is perceived therein, it is "undifferentiated" (*aviveka*). Thus, it is "empty-undifferentiated" (*śūnyāviveka*). It is "made" (*kṛta*) because it is produced according to the principle of making space. It is "Dharma" because its nature consists of the fluid essence of all the qualities of a Buddha. Having thus awakened them with these three words, they urge the goddesses.

Having addressed [the goddesses] with the words "equal" (*samā*), [it means] they are equal to you alone because their nature is your *tathatā*. To the question "Which ones are they?", he says: "Light" (*bhā*) and so forth. She is called "Light" (*bhā*) because she shines eternally due to being present within the body of the Lord; or, because she consists of the assembly of the four goddesses, she is called "Light" (*bhā*) because she shines intensely. [This is] because of her form... [4v]...
It is peace because it pacifies all bodily afflictions;
it is liberation because it releases one from all mental obscurations;
it is sublime bliss because it brings about delight in all the qualities of a Buddha.

These five goddesses are peerless because they perform the welfare of the world through infinite emanations. If they are thus peerless, how is it that they appear in diverse forms such as Bhā-devī and so forth? To this he says: “But [they are] *māyā*s. The meaning of the word “but” (*tu*) is that although they are peerless, they are nonetheless *māyā*s. Just as wood and other materials, when empowered by mantras and the like, manifest in the form of elephants and so on—which are unreal—that is *māyā*; by analogy, the goddesses are also *māyā*s. This is because, within the outflow of the *dharmakāya*—that is, in pure mundane gnosis—they appear in the form of various unreal bodies, speech, and minds.

For what reason are the goddesses called *māyā*? He says: "In order to act" (*kayye*), which means for the sake of the purpose of activity, that is, for the sake of the welfare of the world. And therefore, they are equal to the Buddhas; they are identical with the Buddhas such as Vajrasattva and others. For they too are equal [to them] by way of the *dharmakāya*, and in the *saṃbhogakāya*—which has as its nature the pure mundane gnosis that is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of that [dharmakāya]—they appear in various forms for the sake of performing activities for the welfare of the world. [Question: "In order to act" for what? To this he says: "They sport," and so forth. All the goddesses and Buddhas, who are equal to space, sport. Having come together, they delight in the conduct for the sake of the manifold welfare [of beings].

How do they play? For how long? To this he says: "They are *asa-mā*. *Śama* means tranquility or destruction. Because that [destruction] is absent, they are *aśamā*; for it is said that the Tathāgatas possess an eternal body. Indeed, the Tathāgatas are eternal by way of all three bodies (*kāya*). By the *svābhāvika-kāya*, they are eternal through natural permanence, because they are without beginning or end. By the *sāmbhogika-kāya*, they are eternal through non-interruption, because there is no cessation. By the *nairmāṇika-kāya*, they are eternal through continuity, because even when there is destruction in one place, at that very moment there is arising elsewhere, and because they remain in other places—just like a mass of fire clinging to a great forest.
Aspiration:

Thus, this is an encouragement for the sake of grasping the mind of play, whose intrinsic nature is the enjoyment of the Dharma; for it is eternal because it accomplishes the welfare of the world, is pure, and is free from affliction. Here, the fixed [mantra] is the six-syllable mantra: *rulu rulu bhyo ruṭ*.
2.4 "Illusion," and so forth.
They have the nature of illusion and are equal to the manifested light.
They speak with voices equal in their shared nature;
phenomena are without play, equal to the sky.
By their very nature, they are devoid of union and are like lutes;
they are illusory and lack intrinsic being.

"Equal to space" (*khasamānām*) refers to the Buddhas and goddesses whose nature is the *dharmakāya*. "Phenomena" (*dharmāḥ*) refers to the phenomena of the teaching (*deśanā-dharma*), which are likewise equal to space; the meaning is that they too appear as being equal to space because of their equality with space. For this very reason, they are "without play" (*akrīḍāḥ*). Indeed, those who are equal to space do not play, nor can there be play for those who are equal to space. This is because they appear through illusion as having a nature and form identical [to space], due to such a discernment. "Equal sound" (*tulyaravaḥ*) refers to an echo.

Words have that as their essence; they possess the property of having an identical sound, being equal to those [sounds] because they are mere appearances (*pratibhāsa*). "Assemblage" (*samāgama*) means a collection (*saṃghāta*). Because such a collection does not exist, the phonemes (*varṇa*) are "parts without assemblage" (*asamāgamāṃśā*); thus, the properties (*dharma*) are "parts without assemblage. This is because phonemes are uttered in a sequence and because they perish as soon as they are uttered. Furthermore, phonemes are not combined; they are not denoters, and since they are non-denoters, they are not [independent] properties. Therefore, these properties are equal to space (*khasama*). For this very reason, by their own nature, they are "equal to a lute," meaning they are like the sound of a lute.

Because that [speech] consists of non-expressive words and is devoid of intentional thought (*nirabhisandhi*), it is "equal to the moon in water" (*jalacandrasamā*). Here, *ka* means water; the suffix *ka* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). *Dyota* means the moon. Thus, the meaning is "equal to the moon reflected in water. Alternatively, *dyota* means a lamp; they are equal to one who has performed illumination (*kṛtadyota*). The meaning is that they have become the light of knowledge for the world that has fallen into the darkness of ignorance. Furthermore, by this, their capacity to accomplish the welfare of the world is made known; by the remainder [of the verse], their purity is shown. Therefore, the collective meaning is: "Therefore, you too, having emerged from meditative absorption, teach the Dharmas."
2.5 "That which," and so forth:
that light of the Dharma is equal to space.
The vajras manifest transformations within that [state], equal in form;
they manifest transformations [that bring about] the inexhaustibility of the bliss of desire for forms and so forth.
In that [reality], which is like the moon reflected in the ocean, the Vajra-way is present.

It is the very Dharma of all Buddhas, having become one in flavor (*samarasībhūta*), because it is illumination by virtue of its luminous nature. And it is equal to space because it is free from appearances. Having manifested therein, the Vajras—the Vajrasattvas—perform transformations and display their conduct for the benefit of sentient beings. Are they of the nature of form? No, he says; they are "equal to form," because they define themselves solely as the appearance of form. *rūpasvabhāvāḥ* em., *rūpasvabhāvā* ms.

The method (*naya*) of those *vajras* is the mandala. To the question, "What kind of method is there in that? he says: "Form and so forth," and so on. The five desires are form and the rest; because it bestows inexhaustible bliss through them, it is so described. The "ocean" refers to rivers, ponds, and the like. The "moon" in this [ocean] is the moon itself. It is similar to that [ocean] because it is delimited by its equality with reflections. Thus, all Buddhas, who are equal to space, manifest a body and a bodily mandala for the sake of sentient beings. Therefore, the intended meaning is: "You too should manifest both."
2.6 Regarding "many" (*bahu*) and so forth: [This refers to] the body (*deham*), though the manuscript may read *dehim*.
There, the Vajra Way possesses many seats of yoga;
there, the one who assumes many forms consists of vajra. He emanates sentient beings as equal to himself.
There, Vajra grants boons equal to the elements;
he causes them to expand.

He is so called because he possesses many seats of yoga (*yogapīṭha*). Because he exists within them, he is "consisting of vajra" (*vajramaya*), "of the nature of vajra" (*vajrātmā*), and "the holder of the vajra" (*vajradhara*). By means of the diversity of the dispositions of those to be trained, he maintains [his presence] therein through various forms. From that very source, he emanates beings such as Buddhas who are equal to himself in power, because they are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of him. Therein, by those beings, "Vajra" refers to Vajradhara. "Dei" means he gives. "Varān" means desired things, such as Buddhahood and so forth. "Dhātusamān" means equal to their spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

The meaning is "according to the lineage" (*yathāgotra*). In some recensions, the reading is *jei*; it means "he conquers" (*jayati*) and "he disciplines" (*vinayati*). The meaning there is that he simultaneously and equally [purifies] the excellent elements (*varadhātu*) of the three-thousandfold world systems. The intention is: "O Vajradhara, set such activity for the benefit of others into motion."
2.7 Thus, having taught the *caturgītikā* (four-verse meter) for the four goddesses in order to know the number of the goddesses and so forth, he says "e" and so on to enjoin those very [goddesses].
In each quarter-verse (*pāda*) of these two [verses], there are four groups (*gaṇa*) of four morae (*mātrā*). The [syllables] "āṇei" and "vajja" are short for the sake of filling [the meter].

These are the four goddesses. This song has been proclaimed: "By means of this, impel the Lord of Oneself who is established in the samādhi equal to space; he who hears this song sees it with the body of sound. "With a single mind" means with a concentrated mind. "He penetrates with the body of meaning" means with the mind through verbal expression.

Then, [the author] asks, "What follows from that? and says, "Eha," and so forth. This song is equal to space because it is a manifestation of suchness (*tathatā*). It brings forth Vajradhara who is equal to form. And for that purpose, it awakens—that is, it causes to arise—the mind whose nature is the fluid of Dharma consisting of vajra. By means of a single intrinsic nature, it brings forth the *tantra*, the Vajra Way.
2.9 Now, regarding the origin of Vajra and the Vajra-method, he asks: "What are the mantras? and says: *vajjapaeṇa*, etc.
In this [meter], there are three groups (*gaṇas*) of four morae (*mātrās*) in each quarter-verse.

The *vajrapada* is the seed-syllable of the Vajradhara, namely the syllable *HŪṂ*. By that, the seed is differentiated from other intrinsic natures. The connection is that one meditates upon it from a single seed, which is the fluid of the *dharma*. The meaning is that by means of that very fluid of the *dharma*, one meditates upon the five *HŪṂ*s.
To the question "What is the purpose of that?", he says: "Mind," and so forth. "Mind" refers to the Blue Vajradhara. One meditates upon the entire mandala in which he resides at the center.

In Apabhraṃśa, there are indeed three forms for the word *sarva*. When the letter *r* is elided, there is an option regarding reduplication (*dvirvacana*). In the absence of reduplication, there is either the lengthening of the preceding vowel *a* or the substitution of *ha* for *va*. Thus: *savva*, *sāva*, *sāha*.
To explain how the cultivation of the five seeds arises from the flow of *dharma*, he says: *dhamma*, etc.

This *anuṣṭubh* is named *pathyāvaktra*. Furthermore, in this [meter], two light syllables (*laghu*) shall not occur together after the first syllable in the quarters; for the odd-numbered quarters (*ayujaḥ*), the *ya*-gaṇa occurs after the fourth syllable, while for the even-numbered quarters (*yujaḥ*), the *jas*-gaṇa occurs after the fourth syllable.

The maṇḍala is the gabled pavilion (kūṭāgāra), and the meditation is said to be upon that supreme lotus situated in its center. Likewise, there is the meditation on the Dharma: "The meditation on the supreme purity situated in the middle of the Dharma-maṇḍala. "He contemplates that" means he meditates on the differentiator (bhedaka) of that Dharma; this is the ellipsis. This is because [the Dharma] transforms into the form of the syllable *HŪṂ* mounted upon a moon within the pericarp and the petals of the directions.
Then, what should one do? He says: "Māya," and so forth.
In each quarter of these two [verses], there are three *gaṇas*.

The ellipsis is: "Perform the investigation of all form, which indeed has the nature of *māyā*. O, contemplate the single nature of the mind whose nature is the *vajra*; [contemplate] the *Vajra-way*.

One might object: "Is it not the case that the very nature of the mind is the Vajra-way (*vajranaya*), and not illusion (*māyā*)? To this he says: "O Mind! and so forth. The non-existence of forms (*ākāra*) is due to their being devoid of a nature that is either one or many. Therefore, the mind is of the same nature as space (*kha*). Its discipline (*vinaya*) is the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*). The meaning is that the discipline of the Vajra-way—the way of the mind—is the state of the mind’s own nature being without intrinsic nature; that is to say, its lack of a [real] form, its falsity. Discipline (*vinaya*).

Now, one might object: "Is not the Vajra one thing and the Vajra-method another, given the difference in their appearances? How then can they have a single nature? To this he says: "Both," and so forth. There is no method—that is, no logical principle—for that which possesses a manifold nature, because forms are unreal within the sky-like mere luminosity. When one abides in that state, the Vajra itself—the Holder of the Sky-like Vajra—is the very nature; everything else is illusion, due to its unreality.
2.13 *vajrasattva* and so forth:
in each quarter-verse of these two [metres], there are four groups (*gaṇa*), each consisting of four morae (*mātrā*).

By the first [verse], he speaks of the artificial and non-artificial form; by the second, of the secret of mind and speech. "O Vajrasattva, you are of a single nature; for the sake of the world, you manifest as an illusory nature"—the word "by you" is to be supplied. How so? He says: "O Being," and so forth. That by which beings are disciplined is "discipline" (*vinaya*), which refers to a particular manifestation of form. It awakens beings; thus, its nature is discipline (*vinayasvabhāva*).
2.14 O Vajrasattva, you are by nature of one single essence.
*vajrasattva tvam*] em., *vajrasattvam* ms.

The Goddess speaks (bollaï) to Bhādevī: "O Vajra," that is, to Vajradhara. "Aho Guha" means secretly or hidden; the meaning is that [the deity] exists in the form of a secret of mind and speech. "In the interior" (abbhantare) means in one's own heart. "Ramantaüṃ" means sporting; by way of the nature of the mind, in the form of the universal vajra situated upon the lunar disc. "Tahi ja" means indeed in the heart. "Cittanigūḍha" means concealed within the hub (varaṭaka) of the universal vajra. "Dhammaï siṭṭhaüṃ" means the mantra is also emitted, and that is the syllable HŪṂ.

2.15–16 Regarding the expansion (*spharaṇa*), he says: "The expansion," and so forth. In one [verse], there are eight *mātrās* in the odd [pādas] and twelve in the even; in the other, there are fourteen in the odd and twelve in the even.

The heart-mantra, the vajra, expands [the visualization] of sentient beings who are of the nature of space and like an illusion; then it reabsorbs them. Because the nature of the mind is one, when the mind is examined, since indeed everything is seen to be equal and identical by virtue of its being like an illusion, I repeatedly make the gathered and reabsorbed sentient beings of a single form.

% Excursus on the Sādhana By all of this, the following is stated: Here, preceded by the sevenfold unsurpassed worship, taking refuge, and the generation of the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), one should resolve upon the state of mind-only (*cittamātratā*). Having brought the spirit of enlightenment, which is equal to space, before oneself, one should consecrate [it] with: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness. Thereafter, one should visualize the goddess Cundā, born from the syllable *cuṃ*, white as the moon, four-armed, holding a bowl with her hands in the gesture of meditative concentration (*samādhimudrā*).

Having visualized her holding a rosary and a book in her other two arms, wearing a crown of matted locks, seated in the vajraparyaṅka posture upon a great lotus moon, and equal in size to the world-system; and having visualized within the pericarp of that lotus— which is as clear and white as a pearl and possesses the form of the source of phenomena (dharmodayā)— a peaked pavilion (kūṭāgāra) produced from the syllable *Bhrūṃ* and transformed from Vairocana, consisting of five most brilliant jewels, square, with four doors, adorned with four archways,
and featuring on its four altars throngs of Apsarases busily engaged in beautiful worship.
Adorned with necklaces, half-necklaces, silk bands, garlands, chowries, and other ornaments,
it resounds with the ringing of bells and the tops of banners fluttering in the wind.

Having meditated thus, one should visualize an eight-petalled red lotus in its center; within its pericarp, upon a solar disc, one should contemplate the Blessed One Akṣobhya, produced from the syllable *HŪṂ*, resembling a sapphire, wearing a crown of matted hair marked by a jewel, slightly wrathful with bared fangs, adorned with variegated garments and ornaments, and embracing his own consort with both arms holding a vajra and a vajra-bell. Having visualized him, one should draw the Tathāgatas from all directions by means of the sound of illusory union, cause them to enter through the mouth, and dissolve them into the interior of the lotus, contemplating them as consisting of great bliss. [One should contemplate them] as having entered the interior of the lotus.

Having observed that his parents have dissolved into its radiance, one should see that lotus filled by the *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas, as if by the liquid of the moon. Following that, the four deities— Śānti, Mokṣā, Suṣamā, and Asamā— seated upon the moons at the four gates, should exhort Mahāvajradhara, who consists of the *dharmakāya*, by means of a fourfold song for the purpose of rousing him from that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the great bliss of liberation free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
The Dharma practiced by those who have attained emptiness is equal;
peace, liberation, and perfect equanimity are peerless.
Indeed, those who possess no deceit are equal to the Buddhas.
They sport, equal to all, yet peerless.
2.3 The augment *ruṭ* is added after [the suffix] *luru* when two [syllables] follow.
They speak of the nature of illusion as being equal to the power of karma, and as being equal to the dharmas that possess identical characteristics.
Phenomena are like froth, like bubbles;
they are equal to a mirage, and like a vain assembly.
2.4 The augment *ruṭ* is applied after [the root] *luru* when followed by two [consonants].
Those who possess the eye of Dharma and are like a wish-fulfilling tree perform what is blameless there, being like a form; for they have exhausted the pleasure of sensual desires such as form.
One must avoid that which is like a water-moon.
2.5 After the two [suffixes] *lur* and *luṅ*, the augment *ruṭ* is inserted.
Many are the obstacles there to be avoided; many are the forms assumed there that must be shunned.
One should sever the seven internal enemies, equaling oneself [to others].
Therein, it bestows the fault that is like excellent dust.
2.6 The suffix *ruṭ* is added after the two [roots] beginning with *lur*.
Having thus sung these songs, the four goddesses enter and dissolve into the fluids in the petals of their respective directions, becoming of one flavor.

And in accordance with the *gītikā*, by means of that lunar fluid, there should be five *hūṃ* syllables on the moon-seats in the pericarp and the eastern petals and so forth, being blue, white, dark-blue, red, and green respectively. One should contemplate a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) at the *hūṃ* in the pericarp, and five-pronged vajras of the same color as the *hūṃ*s in the east and other directions. By the radiation of rays from the seed-syllable arisen within the central hub, one performs acts for the benefit of the world; then those vajras transform into the forms of the six deities as appropriate.

Therein, through the transformation of the seed-syllable *viśvavajra*, there appears the Blessed Lord Vajrasattva. Resembling a sapphire, he wears a crown of matted hair, possesses the bloom of youth, and is adorned with various garments and ornaments. Seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, he stands embracing his own consort with both arms, which hold a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) and a bell marked with a double-vajra. He embodies the heroic and erotic sentiments (*vīra-śṛṅgāra-rasa*). On the eastern petal, from the seed-syllable of a white vajra, arises Śānti, who is white in color.

On the southern petal is Mokṣā, blue in color, arisen from the seed-syllable of the blue vajra. On the western petal is Suṣamā, the color of a ruby, arisen from the seed-syllable of the red vajra. On the northern petal is Asamā, the color of emerald, arisen from the seed-syllable of the green vajra. These four are in the bloom of youth, embodying the sentiments of love and heroism; they wear jeweled crowns, various garments and ornaments, and gaze with smiling sidelong glances at the Blessed One. With their right hands, they hold vajras marked with five points of their respective colors; with their left hands, they hold a wheel, a red lotus, a white lotus, and a blue lotus. They sit in the sattva-paryaṅka posture.

Thereafter, having visualized a blue syllable *hūṃ* emitting garlands of light within the moon at the center of the *viśvavajra* between the breasts of the Blessed One and the Goddess Bhā, one should consecrate oneself with the thought: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Dharmadhātu*. Then, having contemplated white, red, and black syllables *oṃ*, *āḥ*, and *hūṃ* upon the moons at the head, throat, and heart, one should consecrate them with the mantras: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Body-Vajra of all Tathāgatas*; *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Speech-Vajra of all Tathāgatas*;
*Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Mind-Vajra of all Tathāgatas*.

One should visualize one’s own seed-syllable within the moon at the center of the five-pronged vajra of the same color situated upon the moon between the breasts of the four goddesses, and likewise the *praṇava* (oṃ) and other syllables within the moons of the head, throat, and heart. Then, having ascertained that the body, speech, and mind of all deities are, according to reality, equal to space, formless, unarisen due to the absence of substantiality, and devoid of intrinsic nature, one should consecrate them with this verse:
“Form is the syllable of the body, unarisen; speech and mind are without characteristics.”

"It is a false collection, consisting of the conceptualization of the vajra of space. (GST 17.36) Then, having brought the circle of gnosis (*jñānamaṇḍala*) by means of the radiance of one's own seed-syllables extending through the ten directions, and having stationed it in the air in front [of oneself], one should offer the water for honor (*argha*) recited at one's heart. Having drawn in, caused to enter, bound, and subjugated the circle of gnosis with these syllables—*jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, *hoḥ*—one should visualize the circle of commitment (*samayamaṇḍala*) as having become one with it.

Then, having resolved that one is being consecrated by Tathāgatas drawn forth by the rays of the heart-mantra, who hold precious vases filled with the water of gnosis, one should visualize the Family Tathāgatas within the crowns of the deities produced from that water.

There, upon the crown of his own matted locks, he visualizes the Blessed One Akṣobhya, resembling sapphire, standing in the earth-touching gesture (*bhūsparśamudrā*). Upon his forehead is Vairocana, resembling moonlight, standing in the gesture of supreme enlightenment (*bodhyagrīmudrā*). Upon his right ear is Ratnasaṃbhava, golden in color, standing in the gesture of granting boons (*varadamudrā*). Upon the back of his neck is Amitābha, resembling a ruby, standing in the gesture of meditative concentration (*samādhimudrā*).

One should visualize Amoghasiddhi, with the luster of emerald, upon the left ear, standing in the *abhaya* (protection) mudrā. Likewise, one should meditate on Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Amitāyus, and Amoghasiddhi, respectively, atop the jeweled crowns of the four goddesses of Bhāva.

Then, by means of the radiation of goddesses emerging from the rays of light from the heart-mantra, which pervade the expanse of the sky through the yoga of emanation, one should worship the Blessed One together with his retinue.

Having then worshipped according to the rules with the secret worship and the worship of the five essences (*vīrya*), one should consecrate [the deity] with: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the worship of all Tathāgatas."
Then, with three verses through the mouths of the four goddesses, one should praise the Blessed One:
"O you who wear the crown of the five Buddhas, whose essence is the three worlds, and who have attained the state of primordial Buddhahood—
may your infinite power be like the sky."

merit becomes infinite;
by proclaiming the seven vices, the greatness of the Dharma is attained.

Then, having emanated all the Tathāgatas from the mouths of the light rays of the heart-mantra and having made the world consist of that [nature], one should contemplate the mind’s nature as the universal form (*viśvarūpatā*). Again, having withdrawn them, one should perceive the mind’s single-naturedness (*ekasvabhāvatā*).

In this tantra, the conventional usage of the three samādhis does not exist; here there is only one samādhi, named Maṇḍalarājāgri. [End of section] || o || When weary from meditative cultivation, one should recite the mantra. The mantra is the heart-mantra *HŪṂ* located within the hub of the double-vajra (*viśvavajra*), or the near-heart-mantra. Or: *anurāgayāmi HŪṂ*; or: *ubhayam anurāgayāmi HŪṂ*; or the seventeen-syllable mantra: *OṂ MAHĀSUKHA VAJRASATTVA JAḤ HŪṂ VAṂ HOḤ SURATASTVAṂ*. Or one should recite other mantras, vidyās, and so forth, as appropriate.
Then one should make aspirational prayers; briefly, however, by means of two verses:
"By these roots of virtue, may I attain the state of all the Buddhas, the holders of the great vajra, and may I cause the entire world to attain it as well."
May I attain that conduct for the sake of perfect awakening, which has been praised by the Perfectly Awakened Ones and by Bodhivajra; may that twofold conduct be mine.

Then, having internalized the pledge-maṇḍala drawn forth by the rays of light from the mantra at one's own heart, and having arisen from that state, one should dwell at ease with the sense of identity as one’s own deity within oneself, and by means of the meditative resolve (*adhimokṣa*) upon the four goddesses within the four elements. This is the commencement during the first twilight. This is the commencement during the first twilight.

During the interval between the twilight sessions (*sandhyā*), however, one should instantaneously take as one's object of focus the self in the form of the deity together with the vidyā, as entirely accomplished. Then, having sequentially emitted the four goddesses from the mantra at one’s own heart and established them in their respective places, one should perform everything—the empowerment of the body and so forth—as before.

Thus, at the final twilight session, having worshipped the gnosis-maṇḍala (*jñānamaṇḍala*) and offered the water of honor (*argha*), one should dismiss it with "Oṃ Vajra Mur" and, having performed self-protection, dissolve the commitment-maṇḍala (*samayamaṇḍala*) into one’s own mantra.

At the time of sleep, one should fall asleep having brought face-to-face the infinite, non-manifesting gnosis (*jñāna*). One should arise from sleep when exhorted by the four goddesses and their four songs.
In this manner, one should practice every day until one perceives the signs of accomplishment (*siddhi*).

The mandala of speech (*vāṅmaṇḍala*) is to be explained. Speech is wisdom (*prajñā*), and mind is skillful means (*upāya*). The non-dual state of wisdom and skillful means is the mandala of speech; and that is primarily characterized by wisdom.
Therefore, in order to introduce that, the goddess Bhāṣā says "dia" and so forth.
In this [verse], there are four groups of four morae (caturmātra) per foot across three lines of two feet (dvipadikā).

The twice-born (dvija), meaning Brahmins, and the outcastes (caṇḍāla) possess an identical nature, because they consist of mere consciousness (vijñānamātra) and because their distinguishing forms do not exist. By this example, the Buddha has declared that the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and primordial state (prakṛti) of all phenomena is mere luminosity, equal to space.

[Objection: But surely, even though entities possess multiple intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), they are established by appearance; indeed, even a single nature is so established, for that which is not of the nature of luminosity cannot appear. Therefore, how can you proclaim its oneness and deny its plurality? [Reply: To this he says, "One," and so forth. The state of being mind-only (*cittamātratā*) is the established reality of that [mind] as a single intrinsic nature, because it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). It is not manifold, because the manifold is merely imagined (*kalpita*). When that [single nature] exists, the Vajrī (the Holder of the Vajra) speaks of an identical intrinsic nature.

He states another example with the words beginning "brāhmaṇa" (the Brahmin). A Brahmin and a dog possess a single nature (*ekasvabhāva*), because both the bones and the clothing—such as bracelets and earrings—are illusory (*māyābhūta*). "Vajjapaüṃ" means that which is to be performed slowly; the "vajra-word" is the firm form, which is mind-only (*cittamātratā*). Within that [state], the Brahmin, the dog, and so forth, are the truth, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Now, he asks: by whom has that identical nature been seen there? He replies: "maï joia," meaning "seen by me. (Note: This is the spelling for *kukkura*. 3.3

He states another example, beginning with *mutta* and so forth. *Devī* means goddess. *Tahiṃ* means in that state of having a single nature (*ekasvabhāvatā*). It should be completed with *joasabhāve* (in the nature of light), which is to be supplied in a slow [meter]. *Yoga* is meditative absorption (*samādhi*). *Tahiṃ* means in that yoga. *Savva tumha* means all of you—the four goddesses; this is the meaning. Being of a single nature with *bhāva*, that is, Vajrasattva, you shine. *Prabhāva* means the body, in the sense that it is manifested or displayed; thus, the meaning is "having one body. *Tulla* and so forth... [continues].
In this [verse], there are fourteen mātrās in each quarter.

It has a uniform nature because of its semi-liquid state (*ardhadravatva*). "Of one mind" means having a single mantra. "Vajra, may he awaken; Vajrasattva, may he awaken. "The sole person" means solitary. If it is asked, "Where have the mother and father gone?", he says: "There," and so forth. In that *dharmadrava*, the two—hatred and its intrinsic nature—which are Akṣobhya and Vidyā, have perished. "By half a limb" means by half a body. The power (*prabhāva*) of the Dharma, which is Vajrasattva, is the manifestation (*prabhāvanā*).
Some recite only the phrase *addheṃ aṅgeṃ*; for them, the fourth quarter would consist of sixteen mātrās.
Thus [it is].
He asks, "What is the other half? and says: *vajjadāru*, etc.

In *vajjadāru*, there are three groups (*gaṇa*) of four morae (*mātrā*) in each quarter-verse. In *vajjaho*, due to its shortness, it consists of four morae. A "group" (*gaṇa*), however, consists of three morae when pronounced slowly (*vilambita*).

"Vajradārā" means the Vajra-consort (vajrabhāryā), that is, Bhagavatī. She is bestowed upon the Yogin during that manifestation of the Dharma; she is of one nature and one body with the Vajra, the Holder of the Vajra, because she fills his left half as his very own consort (svābhā).

When does her arising occur? He says: "vajjaho," and so forth. As long as the description and praise is being performed by the four goddesses through the four songs (*caturgītaka*) with the *jhaṇajhaṇā* sound of the Vajra—the fluid of the Dharma—so long [does this occur]. Immediately after that, what is the manifestation of the Dharma? It continues.

Then, regarding where the four goddesses go with the water, he says: "The Lord" (*devaho*), and so forth. The meaning is that one should see them as unified with the left half of the Lord Vajrasattva—that is, with the portion belonging to the goddesses.

Now, one might object: "Vajrasattva is to be meditated upon by us; however, this [water] is something else entirely, being neither female nor male. To this he replies: "Vajrasattva," and so forth. One should pay homage to and meditate upon this very Vajrasattva. Let my word be taken as authoritative, for the intention is that I too am that very Blessed One.
This is what is meant by that *sādhana*.
What is this?

Having actualized the *bodhicitta* equal to space through the sequence of the sevenfold unsurpassed worship, one should visualize the Blessed Lady Cundā with a body three thousandfold in measure by means of the syllable *Oṃ*. Within the pericarp of her lotus, one should contemplate a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) produced from the transformation of Vairocana. In its center, upon the pericarp of a red eight-petaled lotus and a solar disc, one should meditate on the Blessed Lord Akṣobhya, joined in union with his consort. Having caused all the Buddhas to enter and dissolve [into him], and having beheld them situated within the interior of the lotus, [one should remain] right there.

Having seen that wisdom and means have dissolved and become of one flavor (*samarasībhūta*), one should contemplate the seed-syllable at the hub of a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) produced from a red *hūṃ* syllable. This arises within a moon-maṇḍala born from the withdrawal of the flow of Dharma prompted by the four goddesses and their four songs. One should meditate on the Blessed One as the transformation of that [seed-syllable], bearing a male form with his right half and the form of the goddess Bhā with his left half; he resembles a ruby (*padmarāga*), has a prominent breast on the left, is adorned with locks of hair on his forehead in the left half, wears a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭin*), and is arrayed in various ornaments and garments.

Having contemplated the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*), one should visualize the four goddesses entering that very left half [of the body] and becoming of one flavor (*ekarasa*). The remainder—the crown of the five Buddhas and so forth—should be understood as before, according to the appropriate application.
Thus has been described the chapter illuminating the mandala of speech.

The body-maṇḍala is to be explained.
In that regard, the supreme commitment (*samaya*) is the nourishment of the body by means of the body; he speaks of it starting with "the elephant," and so forth.
In each quarter-verse of these two [stanzas], there are four metrical feet (*gaṇa*).

"Of the nature equal to space" refers to one who possesses the yoga of Vajrasattva. "O *joi*" means O yogin. "Accompanied by the mind of cultivation" means with the mind of meditative development. "One-pointed mind" means a single-mindedness; "by that single-mindedness toward the Vajra-holder, one succeeds. Regarding "in form, like all," there is a reading in some versions as "rūvasamāṇa," which means "by similarity of form"; such is the meaning therein. (4.3–6)
Then Śāntideva speaks of suchness (tathatā) by means of four verses, because that [reality] has suchness as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Since these [verses] have suchness as their intrinsic nature, there are three metrical feet (gaṇas) for each line.

"Kunantaü" means "of those who act. "Ea" means "thus," as he will explain. "Dhamma samā" means "the dharmas are equal. "Samīaü" means "let them be gathered"; let them be correctly understood; although there is a plural sense, the singular form is used. "Eaviāra" means "such a deliberation" or "certainty. This deity is Vajrasattva; [he is] Vairocana, the Eternal One. There are five goddesses; these possess a single nature.

One might object: "Should he not be called Akṣobhya rather than Vairocana? To this, he says: "Equal," and so forth. For the yogin of equanimous mind, the Dharma-body, which is of a single flavor, is accomplished. Therefore, his power does not arise here from the sentient being Akṣobhya; rather, it arises from Vairocana, because [Vairocana] illuminates equality by subverting established constraints. Now, what is the benefit in arising from Vairocana?

In order to conclude the reality of the body-maṇḍala (*kāyamaṇḍalatattva*), he says: "O Vajrasattva," and so forth. All these are to be contemplated as having a single nature. How? As before, within the lotus at the pericarp of Cundā, in the central seat-lotus of the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) transformed from Vairocana, there is the melting of Vairocana and his consort through the fluid born of their union. Having arisen after the four goddesses have dissolved, one meditates upon the white Vajradhara born from a white *hūṃ* syllable on a moon disc produced from the solidification of that fluid. From this single-natured Dharmakāya comes the Vajra-way (*vajranaya*), which is the Vajrayāna.
If so, what is the meaning of *yogapīṭha*? To this he says: "Cundā," and so forth. (*yoga°] em., yo yoga° ms.)

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the primordial essence (*prakṛti*), which is the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of all phenomena (*bhāva*, *sarvadharma*), is Cundā. To the question, "What does Vajrasattva do therein? he says: "In that seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*), being embodied and possessing a body, he perceives the single intrinsic nature of all phenomena. "Bhāvaṇa" means cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Vairocana is the Eternal (*śāśvata*). "Deviho" means the truth of the Goddess, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the Vajrin; his arising (*utpatti*). For arising occurs by means of the body (*kāya*), and the body is the Eternal; therefore, he alone explains the arising. How so? He says: "E sasī," etc. This consists of two *dvipadikā* verses.

Here, the odd [syllables] consist of fourteen mātrās each, and the even [syllables] consist of twelve mātrās each. *E* refers to the Yogin. *Sasimaṇḍalamajjhaṭṭhiu* means situated in the center of the moon-maṇḍala born from the withdrawal of the fluid of Dharma (*dharmadrava*). The mantra of the Vajra—that is, of the Vajradhara—is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) white *HŪṂ*. With one-pointed mind, he visualizes the Vajra by means of that mantra. *Tisū* means having three prongs on each side; the meaning is that it has twelve prongs. *Tisūi*? [Note: This appears to be a variant or scribal repetition.]

"Jalantaüṃ" means "blazing"; in some recensions, the reading is "jvalat. "Cittaï vajjasahāva" means "one perceives the nature of the vajra" and "vibhāvai eamaṇa" means "one contemplates this mind. "Tisūi vajja jalantaüṃ" [is another reading]. There too, the meaning is the same; however, with "tisū," there would be no four-mora *yamaka* due to the rapid (druta) meter. "Majjhaṭṭhiaüṃ" means "situated in the middle"; the suffix *-ka* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). "Vajjasahāva" refers to the form of Vajradhara. "Emmaï" means "thus by me. "Vajranayo" is the arising of Vajradhara. "Dhammaüṃ" means "of the dharmas."
