5.1–3: [An objection is raised: "Let the deity arise from the *dharmakāya* itself; what is the use of a mantra? To this, he says: "Non-existence," and so forth.
Here, there are three groups of two syllables each, and the fourth is a group of three. "Non-existence" (*abhāvam*) is four *mātrās* due to its rapid pronunciation.

Because it is uttered rapidly, non-existence is non-conceptual meditative absorption (*samādhi*); existence is the body. It is neither cultivated nor spoken. For even upon waking from a dream, one does not run toward a conceptualization that is itself unarisen. Likewise, even from the *dharmakāya*, there is no arising of a body without the mantra.

*Ammahō* is an address to a woman. *Bhāva* is the mantra, because it brings about (*bhāvayati*) or determines (*nirūpayati*). *Ea* means "in this way," that is, by means of the mantra. *Dhamma niruvajjaü* means "when the Dharma is being determined. *Cittād* means from the non-conceptual state mediated by the mantra. *Bhāva* is the body. By the passage beginning with *cittaho bhāve*, he states another argument: from the non-proliferated (*niṣprapañca*) mind alone, in the state of the body, there is no method (*naya*), that is, no liberation. For that reason, the *bhāva*—the mantra—is performed. *nāsti* em., *nasti* ms.

To the question "Why does it not exist?", he says: "Existence," and so forth. "Existence" (*bhāva*) refers to the body. For the mind, which has that [body] as its intrinsic nature, there is no "way" (*naya*), that is, liberation. This is because of contradiction. What kind of way? It is that intrinsic nature of the mind which is equal to space, resulting from the complete exhaustion of the representations (*vijñapti*)—which manifest as the support, the body, and objects of enjoyment—together with their seeds, through the power of the momentum of the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*).

If it is argued that "that very same embodied being will exist once again," he says: "The mind," and so forth. The mind of one who is being liberated becomes particularly purified; it is exhausted through non-returning. What is that? "Just as before": just as previously, prior to the teaching, there was delusion and the appearance of the causes of delusion.

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "How," and so forth. How can there be the existence of that body and so on, once they have been exhausted through non-return? It is not possible, because of the contradiction. If that is the case, then let the very nature of the mind be its form; therefore, even a purified mind will arise in the form of a body.

Here he says: "It is perfected," and so forth. This is neither a [conventional] entity (*bhāva*) nor is it a body. The *naya*—the ultimate reality—is perfected as either external or consisting of the nature of mind, because it is devoid of a nature that is either one or many. Consequently, the mind has the very nature of space, since mental forms (*ākāra*) are unreal. Unreal appearance is delusion (*bhrānti*). And since there is no delusion for a liberated mind, how could it have a body?

Therefore, from that fluid *dharmakāya*, a consciousness arises as its natural outflow (*niṣyanda*), appearing as a body and so forth; the meaning is that it discerns its own form as false and itself as being like an illusion.

Summarizing, he says: "In my," and so forth. The suffix *ka* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). From the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) arises conceptualization (*vikalpa*); from that, the body—by this reasoning. In the middle, in the interval, the word is the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*) which determines [the form]. Thus, from the mind—which is free of conceptualization and mediated by mantra—the entity, the body, is produced. In this way, Vajrasattva arises, possessing various natures such as the mind-maṇḍala and so forth.
5.4 It has been stated: "Having cultivated [compassion] toward all sentient beings, one should act for the sake of liberation.
And since that liberation is mind-only and of a single flavor, he explains what kind of state it should be cultivated: *achaüṃ*, etc.
In each quarter-verse of this [meter], there are three *gaṇas*.

"Clear" (*accha*) because of its natural purity; "stainless" (*nirmala*) because adventitious stains have been eliminated. By analogy with water, "water" means that which has been melted by the bliss of pliancy (*prasrabdhi*). "Tetthaho" means: in that generation of Vajrasattva. "Laghu" means quickly; "bhāventem" means by that state, by that which has been made into a body. "Emmaï" means: this has been [done] by me. "Kahia nirutta": "akathya" (unfit to be told) has been "kahia" (told); the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*). "Nirutta" means that which has emerged from what was spoken;
the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of "emerged" (*niṣkrāntam*). 5.5.
By the words "The secret of the vajra is unspeakable," and so forth, he states the *samaya*.
In this [verse], there are four lines consisting of four syllables each. In "some," the vowel *e* is short. In "āhāreṃ," the initial vowel is short.

"Somena" means by means of *bodhicitta*. "Bhāva" refers to one's own body. "Tahiṃ" means when that exists. "Vajrodaka" is wine. "Evaṃsvabhāvam" means having the nature of *bodhicitta*. "Cittasahāva" refers to one who abides in the yoga of Vajrasattva.
5.6 *Dhamma*, etc.
The quarters of these two [meters] consist of three gaṇas each.

Dharma, Saṃgha, and Vajrodaka—these have an identical nature. For Vajrodaka is indeed the bodhicitta; that itself is Dharma because it is the Noble Path, and that itself is Saṃgha because it comprises all noble individuals (āryapudgala). Furthermore, the nature of the *vasā* and so forth is identical to the bodhicitta, since phenomena (*dharma*) are mere appearances and their forms are unreal. [The phrase] "the entity is sold" refers to the practice or the intention of the yogins; this is the remainder [of the sense].% 5.7

"Eatable, drinkable, bedding, and seating"—"savvaü" means of all these. Furthermore, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that has been explained is the circle of the mind (*cittamaṇḍala*) and so forth, which arises from the fluid of the Dharma; and its single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is precisely the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
5.8 Now, as for how this arisen, embodied Vajrasattva is to be perceived, he says "Buddha," and so forth.

*Buddha*: Its feet consist of four syllables. There is lengthening at the beginning of *abhāva*. "By the Buddha" means by one who sees everything through the state of awakening (*bodhana*). It is so called because its nature is such that the three—body, speech, and mind—are of the form of awakening (*bodhi*). It is performed; it is seen. In the ultimate sense, what is it like? It is so called because its nature (*prakṛti*) or essence is the non-existence of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-abhāva*), a gnosis equal to space. The meaning is that this is due to the non-existence of [conceptual] forms. *Vajra* refers to the Vajra-holder. By him, the illusory nature (*māyā-svabhāva*) is declared, because of such a thorough discernment.

It becomes equal to space, yet appears as if possessing form; for, while being equal to space, it manifests as if having material form. Others, however, do not recite the fourth quarter, asserting that this [verse] consists of only three quarters.
5.9 With the words *māa* and so forth, he states the result:
in this [meter], the feet consist of three *gaṇas*.

Dharma is intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For one who discerns that the intrinsic nature of illusion is [the reality], the vajra—the *dharmakāya*—is made manifest; this is its preliminary stage or introduction, for its attainment is inevitable. He states the fault in the opposite case with the words beginning "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth. "Existence" is the intrinsic nature of form and so on. Whoever conceives of this possesses the intrinsic nature of a sentient being (*sattva*); for him, there is no method, that is, no *dharmakāya*. Now, if he conceives of this as mind alone, even for that mind, this alone remains its essential core and what is logical: namely, its resemblance to an illusion, because mental aspects (*ākāra*) are unreal. (5.10–11)
Concerning the radiation and reabsorption [of light], he says "ea" and so forth.
The feet of these two [verses] consist of four gaṇas.

First, the mind is made equal to Mount Meru by virtue of its loftiness, vastness, and luminosity. It should not be too vast nor too lofty, for that would lead to distraction; nor should it be dark, for that would lead to lethargy and drowsiness. Subsequently, that mind arises.
[The term] *prabhāsvaratayā* is an emendation; the manuscript reads *prabhāsuratayā*.
"Pure Buddha" means consisting solely of the Buddha because it is pervaded by the emanations (*spharaṇa*) of all the Tathāgatas.

Afterwards, when that mind becomes weary, the mantra-practitioner withdraws it. When that withdrawal occurs, the practitioner recollects and meditates, discerning his own mind as having the nature of Vajradhara through the withdrawal of all the Tathāgatas.

Thereafter, one inflames the mind, which is like Mount Meru, in the form of a mass of light. Within that heap of light, one moves Vajrasattva in bodily form by filling [the space] with hundreds of thousands of millions of his bodies.
Thereafter, having inflamed it, one emanates the form of space through the gradual withdrawal of the bodies of the Vajra-holders. Such is the nature of emanation and withdrawal; this is the summary.
If it is argued that it is logical because the Tathāgatas themselves emanate from the withdrawal of the Tathāgatas, he says: *sijjha*, etc.
Here, there are two triple gaṇas (*trigaṇa*) consisting of odd syllables (*ayuja*), and two double gaṇas (*dvigaṇa*) consisting of even syllables (*yuja*).

Success is achieved in that mind through the single flavor of Vajrasattva and the withdrawal of all Tathāgatas; therefore, emanation as well is logical. [The author] states the time of emanation by Vajradhara with the words beginning "firm" (*sthira*).
In this context, the odd [breaths] are ten measures long and the even ones are twelve measures long.

The yogi expands that which is stable; he should never expand that which is unstable. To expand what is unstable means that the exertion becomes fruitless; the sense is that one would neither obtain the result nor would there be any benefit from the effort.
In order to proclaim that accomplishment (*siddhi*) is easily attained in this tantra, he speaks the six *dvipadī* verses beginning with "savva" and so forth. Here, the feet consist of three *gaṇas*.

"All that has been spoken by me is true according to the literal expression"—this is the ellipsis here. "Established" (*siddha*) means established by nature; "vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to the path to enlightenment, which possesses its own being and reality.
If it is argued, "Granted that this vehicle is established by nature, but our mind is defiled," he says: "The mind," and so forth.
This is the two-line verse of the *Dvipathaka*:

"Do not defile the mind, for it is equal to space due to its natural purity (*prakṛti-śuddhatva*). It is equal because that nature is unchanging. To the question "How so?", he says: "Because no impurity can stain it," since impurities are adventitious (*āgantuka*) to that nature, like smoke, darkness, clouds, or frost in the sky.
With the words "joi" and so forth, he states the power of the deity;
here, the feet consist of three *gaṇas*.
(Note: *trigaṇāḥ* is the emendation; the manuscript reads *trigāṇāḥ*.)

These are the yogins. This Blessed Lady Cundā, whose intrinsic nature is primordial, gives birth to all Buddhas. When the vajra-power has been cultivated—where "power" (*prabhāva*) means radiance, splendor, or production—if she gives birth to the Buddhas, one might ask, "What is the use of Vajradhara? To this, he says: "The Goddess," and so forth.
In this [meter], there are four groups of four syllables per line.
The goddesses and the Vajra-holder deity possess one and the same nature; these [goddesses] are merely its manifestations (*vibhūti*).

One might then ask: "What is the purpose of the Buddhas? To this he says: The Blessed Vajrasattva is the very power, manifestation, and essence of the Buddhas, because his nature is the *dharmakāya*. For this very reason, he is the root of the Buddhas who are comprised within the two bodies (*kāya*). Furthermore, because the *dharmakāya* is without beginning or end, he alone is the root. Thus, he is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddhas of the three times who are subsumed within the Vajra-holder; this is the power of the deity.

5.18 He speaks of the power of intention (*āśayabala*) and the power of mantra (*mantrabala*) with the words beginning "anunaya" and so forth. *Anunaya* is the intention for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings within the mind; its cultivation is what is meant. The form "he" is the substitution of *he* for the third-person singular ending. Through that [cultivation], accomplishment is certain, as well as through the syllable *hūṃ*, which has the sense of conciliation (*anunaya*).

Therefore, indicating that this very yoga should be practiced incessantly with unbroken cross-legged postures (*paryaṅka*), he says: "In the heart" (*hiae a*), and so forth. Here, the feet consist of three *gaṇas*. There is also a long vowel at the end of the word *ūru*. The discursive thought (*vitarka*) regarding the thighs and feet—such as "my thigh is pained" or "my foot is pained"—is futile. It is "delusion" (*moha*) because it obstructs the fruit, and it is "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) because it originates from lack of knowledge. That [discursive thought] is not produced in the heart; it is not fit to be performed within the heart.

Regarding the [verse] beginning with *vajra* (5.20): one might ask, "Since there are indeed obstacles (*vighna*), how then can there be accomplishment? To this he replies: Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, and the other lords of beings in the ten directions, together with their retinues, are the creators of obstacles. The "wheel" (*cakra*) refers to the collection of the three worlds; that [collection] is restrained by the splendors of the vajra. The "splendors of the vajra" (*vajraprabhā*) are the rays of light issuing from the vajra at the heart, which, as they radiate, take the form of blazing vajras. By these [splendors], the [obstacles] are restrained—that is, cast out. Therefore, the sense is that no obstacles have power here.
If it is argued that the destruction of obstacles through the yogas of the wrathful deities is more powerful, he says: "The necklace," and so forth. Here too, the feet consist of three gaṇas.

The yogin emanates thousands of millions of wrathful deities into the expanse of space, [thinking] "the vajra-holder has a single nature. This is through the firm conviction of non-difference from the Vajradhara. Furthermore, he necessarily reabsorbs them by means of their very nature as vajras.

5.22 And because this tantra has as its primary objective the realization of the state equal to space (*khasama*), it is designated by that very name. Therefore, in order to conclude that very subject, he says "citta" and so forth;
this is a two-path [verse].

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the mind is its primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is suchness (*tathatā*); that very [nature] is awakening (*bodhi*), the method (*naya*), and the reality (*tattva*). It is not [the reality] of the stains. Therefore, when those [stains] are exhausted, because that [nature] is inexhaustible, awakening is easily attained. [Objection: But awakening is infinite, and the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*) are [also infinite]; how can they be the reality of that [awakening]? To this, he says: "Of awakening, the method... and so forth. The method and reality of awakening is precisely the intrinsic nature of the mind; it is simply the suchness of the mind. For that alone is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Buddhas, because it is the basis (*āśraya*) of the Buddha-qualities, and not the Buddha-qualities themselves. For those [qualities] are its manifestations (*vibhava*), not its essential form (*svarūpa*).

If, then, suchness alone is the reality for both, and that suchness is emptiness—the absence of duality—then because duality is always and everywhere non-existent, it is an absolute non-existence like the horn of a hare. Furthermore, absolute non-existence cannot be the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of entities, nor can there be a direct perception (*pratyakṣībhāva*) of it, because its nature is non-luminous. To this, he says: "Both," and so forth. Both refers to the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and awakening (*bodhi*). Their intrinsic nature is suchness. And the "mind" (*citta*) of that [suchness] is the method (*naya*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The mind itself, devoid of duality, is the emptiness of duality, because it is designated by means of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) based on that [mind] alone.

If, then, mind itself is emptiness and the mind has been deluded from the very beginning, such that its very nature is [delusion], then delusion itself would be awakening (*bodhi*). But that is incorrect, because awakening is characterized by the total exhaustion of all delusions along with their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). Therefore, he says: "O mind," and so forth. For delusion and the stains which are its causes are adventitious; the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the mind is indeed like space, because it is mere luminosity and because mental forms (*ākāra*) do not exist.

Sometimes by way of setting [of the sun], and sometimes by way of non-existence alone, there is a delimitation in the states of mind belonging respectively to the mundane, the supramundane, and those attained subsequent to them. Precisely because the stains are adventitious, awakening (bodhi) is easily attained; therein, the purification of adventitious stains is that which is to be accomplished, while natural purity is already established.
This chapter illuminates the common meaning found across various tantras and different chapters. ||o||
By this merit, which has attained a beauty as lovely as the autumnal moonlight, acquired through my speech while worshipping the *Śrīmat-tantra*—
which is equal to space— I shall swiftly attain the peerless Brahman, which is equal to space.
Wherein the union of the lights of the qualities prevails for the sake of the universe.
The fifth chapter in the *Khasamā*, a commentary on the *Khasamatantra*. [Fleuron]
This commentary named *Khasama* on the *Khasamatantra* is completed. This work is the composition of the great paṇḍita, the venerable Ratnākaraśānti. [Fleuron]
